extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for producing short and long fiction focused on idea generation, disciplined practice, mastery of craft elements (character, plot, POV, dialogue, theme), and revision. Includes exercises for scheduling, freewriting, and character development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Idea recognition and selection
rubrics_metrics.description: You will know when the right idea has arrived; the 'right idea' will loudly and persistently announce its presence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ideas are plentiful; once you start seeing the world as a writer your problem shifts from lack of ideas to having too many. The right idea may be obvious immediately or take days to reveal itself. Treat ideas as seeds to be cultivated into many interlocking elements (characters, events, setting) rather than expecting one seed to yield a complete story on its own.

rubrics_metrics.name: Record and cultivate ideas (keep a notebook)
rubrics_metrics.description: Write your ideas down; most writers keep a notebook handy because ideas will pop up rapidly and cannot all be remembered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jottings don't have to make sense and you won't use every one, but the notes provide raw material that will later 'flower into something very useful.' Keep a notepad near your bed for ideas that come at night; capture soft-time inspirations immediately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transform seeds into fiction (don't slavishly follow facts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Once you plant real-life seeds in a story, let them grow into fiction rather than confining the story to literal facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fiction demands better storytelling than real life; beginning writers who adhere too rigidly to facts produce stories that feel flat or indulgent. Fictionalizing real events can increase the Truth and deepen impact (example: Lorrie Moore). Use imagination to sharpen focus and shape suspense, clarity, irony, and humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write for a stranger (audience-focus)
rubrics_metrics.description: The goal is to write a story that a total stranger will enjoy; readers don't care about the writer but about a great story well told.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Picture a 'total stranger' reading your work and craft the story to engage that reader. The stranger cares only about entertainment and/or meaning, so prioritize story elements that serve the reader's experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show up for work — discipline and scheduled practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Frequent, regular practice is the best way to get good at writing fiction; set aside designated writing times, preferably most days of the week.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discipline and consistent writing beat intermittent brilliance. Stick to a schedule (more important than producing something wonderful each session). Exercises: create a week-long schedule with at least five hours of writing time, installments at least one hour each, and use it for a week to test and adjust. Some writers measure in pages rather than hours; find what works.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hard time vs soft time
rubrics_metrics.description: There are two kinds of writing time: 'hard time' (actual writing) and 'soft time' (pondering and incubation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both are necessary: hard time is where words get written; soft time includes research, conversations, thinking while doing other activities (walking the dog, errands, bedtime). Use soft time to unblock problems and incubate solutions. Keep materials (notepad, pen) handy to capture ideas generated during soft time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use freewriting and separate creation from revision (Free Spirit vs Stern Editor)
rubrics_metrics.description: In early stages, let the Free Spirit produce fragmentary, rambling material; later invite the Stern Editor to cut, correct, and shape.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Banishing the editor during initial drafting lets ideas flow; freewriting (not lifting pen/fingers) is a kick-start when stuck. After drafting, alternate between the two modes; toward the end, submit to rigorous editing. Practical advice: write freely for a set time (exercise: freewrite for at least five minutes from a given opener).

rubrics_metrics.name: Learn craft (time-tested elements)
rubrics_metrics.description: A working knowledge of craft—showing rather than telling, character, plot, dialogue, point of view, theme, etc.—is necessary to make fiction strong.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Craft rules emerged as guiding principles that make fiction better; they are learnable and make writing easier (less floundering). Examples: replace 'Kathy was a dishonest woman' with a scene showing Kathy pocketing an overchange to illustrate dishonesty. The book focuses on digesting craft elements so they become part of the writer's system.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know the rules before breaking them
rubrics_metrics.description: You can break rules more effectively if you understand them thoroughly first.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Great innovators (e.g., Frank Lloyd Wright, James Joyce, Hemingway) knew structural principles deeply before transgressing them. Use knowledge of craft as foundation for deliberate experimentation rather than ignorance-driven rule-breaking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read widely and analyze (learn from masters and failures)
rubrics_metrics.description: Study the masters and a broad range of writers; read adventurously and analyze what works and what doesn't.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Learn by close reading and imitation (exercise: transcribe a favorite passage word for word to feel how it was created). Ask why a story leaves you cold—plot plausibility? pointlessness? show-offy sentences?—and learn from both admired works and those you dislike.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characters must have a driving desire
rubrics_metrics.description: Every dimensional character should want something; desire provides momentum to drive the story forward.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Desire can be enormous (revenge, easing loneliness) or small (finding a wedge of Brie), but must be strong and concrete. A story grows organically from a character's need; without desire, even brilliant description cannot sustain narrative interest (examples: Katherine Anne Porter's 'Theft'; Nabokov's Lolita; Raymond Carver's 'So Much Water...'). Exercise: pick a character and a single concrete driving desire.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create human complexity (avoid one-dimensional types)
rubrics_metrics.description: Make characters distinct and multi-faceted rather than flat archetypes or types.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transcend types (e.g., 'investment banker') by adding specific, sometimes contradictory, details—anonymous donations, odd phone calls—to make characters feel like real people with histories and memories. Distinctiveness and unique details produce dimensional, believable characters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diagnose and fix story weaknesses
rubrics_metrics.description: When a story underperforms, analyze weaknesses such as lack of plausible plot, pointlessness, or overly showy sentences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a piece leaves you cold, ask concrete questions: Is the plot plausible? Does the story feel pointless? Are the sentences show-offy? Use answers to guide revision and craft learning; sometimes the best lessons come from stories you don't like.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use exercises and deliberate practice to internalize craft
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ targeted exercises (scheduling, freewriting prompts, copying passages, character-desire sketches) to build skills.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The book's 'YOUR TURN' exercises are concrete ways to practice: create a week-long writing schedule (minimum five hours), freewrite from a given opener for at least five minutes, and sketch characters with a single concrete desire. Repetition and specific practice lead to incremental but cumulative improvement.
